name: Puma
confidence_why: one confirmed first-hand source; 2 other works read were silent
catalog_citation: Sharma, Narayan Prasad. 2014. Morphosyntax of Puma, a Tibeto-Burman language of Nepal. PhD thesis, SOAS, University of London. 486 pp. DOI 10.25501/SOAS.00018554 (open mirror https://core.ac.uk/download/653669416.pdf)
catalog_locator: Ch. 2 Phonology, section 2.16.1 'Stress', printed pp. 95-96 = PDF pp. 96-97 (examples (4)-(7)); 2.16.2 'Intonation' p. 96
catalog_quote: Like a number of other Tibeto-Burman languages, Puma has no phonemic tonal contrast. Word stress is predictable from the phonemic shape of words, a pattern that is common in Tibeto-Burman, as Noonan (2003: 7) notes. ... Monosyllabic words such as pronouns, nouns, adverbs, and verbs are always stressed. In glossary entries in the lexicon, stress is indicated by a stress mark [ˈ] before the stressed syllable. Unless otherwise indicated, all Puma words are stressed on the first syllable. ... In words with an initial high back vowel /u/ followed by a nasal /ŋ/, the /u/ remains silent and only /ŋ/ is pronounced ... This means that disyllables beginning with /uŋ/ will be stressed on what is underlying the second syllable, as in: uŋ-bo uŋ-nʌŋ → [’ŋbo ‘ŋnʌŋ] ... ‘My name.’ (Rai et al. 2009: 444) In Puma most infinitive forms of verbs are disyllabic words. These disyllabic verbs as well as disyllabic nouns, pronouns, adjectives, and adverbs receive stress on the first syllable. [ˈkhʌnna] ‘you’ [ˈpuŋ-ma] ‘to go’ [ˈase] ‘yesterday’ [ˈnilo] ‘nice’ [ˈapa] ‘father’ Compound verb forms do not deviate from the above rules, as illustrated in: [ˈsom-tuk-ma] ‘to love’ [ˈman-ma-ken-ma] ‘to forget’ [ˈwass-uŋ-kess-uŋ] ‘I threw.’ [ˈdha-puks-a] ‘He fell.’ [ˈris-i-ŋes-i] ‘She laughed.’

Section "2.16 Suprasegmental features / 2.16.1 Stress" begins on printed p. 95 = PDF p. 96 and its example (7) plus 2.16.2 Intonation are on printed p. 96 = PDF p. 97; extracted text shows "2.16.1 Stress", "Unless otherwise indicated, all Puma words are stressed on the first syllable" and "Compound verb forms do not deviate from the above rules" at that locator, so the stated locator is right. Every sentence in the reported quote appears verbatim in the text: "Like a number o…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No lexical tone; stress is predictable and falls on the first syllable of the word, including disyllabic infinitives, nouns, pronouns, adjectives, adverbs, compound verbs and inflected verb forms (e.g. [ˈsom-tuk-ma] 'to love', [ˈwass-uŋ-kess-uŋ] 'I threw').
new_statements.exceptions: Words beginning with /uŋ-/ (e.g. 1SG.POSS uŋ-) drop the initial /u/ in pronunciation, so stress lands on what is underlyingly the second syllable ([ˈŋbo ˈŋnʌŋ] 'my name'); 'unless otherwise indicated' in the glossary suggests isolated lexical marking but none is listed in the section.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; examples are citation forms and inflected verb words (a whole polymorphemic verb form carries one initial stress). Section 2.16.2 treats intonation separately (rising for polar questions).
new_statements.identity_note: Sharma 2014 describes Puma as spoken in Diplung, Mauwabote, Pauwasera, Devisthan and Cisapani VDCs of Khotang district (plus Udayapur emigrants); no Puma dialect split is named for the stress data (the 'Parbate dialect' mentioned on p. 116 is the author's Nepali, not Puma). Matches puma1239 as a whole.

sources.note: Ch. 2 phonology, section 2.16.1 Stress (pp. 95-96): no phonemic tone; word stress predictable from phonemic shape; all words stressed on the first syllable unless otherwise indicated; monosyllables always stressed; disyllables beginning with /uŋ-/ (silent /u/) surface with stress on the underlying second syllable; compound and inflected verb forms keep initial stress; 2.16.2 covers intonation only (rising for polar questions).
